new_statements.second_reader_evidence: Opened (8 pp., the PDF's metadata gives the title 'Wom Language: Noun classes', author Blench, created 2000-08-20; extracted text page 4 gives '2.3 Tones / There are probably two level tones and a falling tone as in Samba Leek.' (the text drops the final ɔ, a SILDoulosIPA glyph); I rendered p. 4 to PNG and the printed line reads exactly 'There are probably two level tones and a falling tone as in Samba Leekɔ.' — verbatim as quoted, at the stated locator (§2.3, p. 4, paper unpaginated). The whole text has no hit for stress/accent/pitch/intonation ('prominently' on p. 5 is about suffixes). §2 'Phonology of Perema' covers consonants (Table 1), vowels (8 phonemic, no nasalised vowels, length no…
new_statements.rule_in_words: The only phonological description of Perema/Wom treats the language as tonal (tentatively two level tones plus a falling tone, by analogy with Samba Leeko) and says nothing about stress or accent; no rule for word-stress placement exists in any source.
new_statements.exceptions: None; the tone statement itself is hedged ('probably') and by comparison with Samba Leeko (Noss 1976).
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level tone; the paper is a preliminary sketch based on 1986/1989 fieldwork at Wom Baga near Yadim, marked 'DRAFT ONLY'. Nothing on stress, phrase-level prominence or citation forms.
new_statements.identity_note: Blench 2000 describes Perema = Wom (Nigeria), ISO wom, glottocode womn1235 (autonyms Perema/Pere/Pereba), from fieldwork at Wom Baga near Yadim, Adamawa State; Kleinewillinghöfer's data are from the Kádìrɔ̄ (Wɔ̀m bāā) variant at Yadim. Beware a homonym: the 'Wom [w̃ɔ̃̀m] (aka Kam)' of Idiatov et al. 2017 and of the Wikipedia Perema article's transcription is the Kam/Nyingwom language of Mayo Kam, Taraba State (ISO kdx), not this language.

Second-hand from Blench 2000: 'Tone is probably high, low, and falling, as in Chamba Leko.' Nothing on stress. Cites Ethnologue and (mistakenly, for the Kam 'Wom') Idiatov et al. 2017.

sources.citation: Idiatov, Dmitry, Mark Van de Velde, Tope Olagunju & Bitrus Andrew. 2017. Results of the first AdaGram survey in Adamawa and Taraba States, Nigeria. CALL 47, Leiden (33 slides).
sources.note: Not about Perema: its 'Wom [w̃ɔ̃̀m] (aka Kam)' of Mayo Kam is the Kam/Nyingwom language (Jakob Lesage's PhD target). Wikipedia's Perema article wrongly imports this transcription. No stress content.
